opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons that reinforce each other.

The first is that coding is a domain where verification is relatively cheap. You write code, you run it, you run the tests, and you get a signal: it works or it doesn't. That's very different from writing an essay or giving advice, where judging quality is fuzzy and expensive. Reinforcement learning thrives on clear rewards, so once the community figured out how to scale RL on top of strong pretrained models, coding was one of the first places where it really took off.

The second is data and environment. There's an enormous amount of high-quality code on the internet, plus commit histories, issues, pull requests, and discussions of why something was changed. And the environment, a computer with a terminal, a file system, and a compiler, is something we can simulate at scale. You can spin up millions of sandboxes. It's much harder to do that for, say, a real-world business negotiation.

The third is that the people building these models are programmers themselves. The researchers and engineers are also the users. They feel the pain points every day, they know what "good" looks like, and they iterate very fast. That tight feedback loop between builder and user is quite rare.

And then there's the product side. Coding has a very natural path from autocomplete, to chat, to agents that can work on a whole repository for a long time. Each step has been immediately useful, so people adopt it, pay for it, and generate more feedback and revenue, which funds the next round of training. It's a flywheel.

But I'd add one caveat. Coding progress is fast partly because it's the "easy" case for current methods. It's checkable, digital, and well-documented. The more interesting question is how much of what we've learned in coding transfers to messier domains where the reward isn't a passing test. In some sense, coding is a preview of what agents could look like everywhere, but it's also a best-case scenario, and we shouldn't assume everything else will move at the same speed.

r002.rationale: It mentions code from the internet and scalable simulated environments, but does not identify GitHub as the source or say its corpus enables construction of many coding environments.

r003.rationale: It cites programmers as both builders and users, but does not attribute product development to users having relatively uniform coding needs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest explanation is that coding is the one domain where almost everything lined up at the same time. If you think about what reinforcement learning needs to work, you need an environment, you need a reward signal, and you need that signal to be cheap and reliable. Code gives you all three for free. You can run the program, you can run the tests, you can see whether it compiles. Compare that to writing an essay or doing research, where the feedback is slow, noisy, and often subjective. So when the field moved from pretraining-only to pretraining plus RL, coding was naturally the first place where that paradigm paid off in a big way.

The second thing is that the base models were already very strong at code, because GitHub is a huge part of the pretraining corpus. So RL wasn't teaching the model to code from scratch. It was mostly teaching it how to use the knowledge it already had across many steps: plan, write, run, read the error, fix, repeat. That's a much easier problem than learning a skill from zero.

And then there's a third factor people underrate, which is that the users of coding tools are engineers. They give very precise feedback, they build tooling around the model themselves, and they're tolerant of a product that's rough at the edges as long as it saves them time. So the loop from research to product to feedback was extremely short. Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, all of these improved quickly partly because the people using them were essentially co-developing them.

I'd actually frame it as a bit of a historical accident that makes coding look special. It isn't that coding is uniquely suited to intelligence. It's that coding happened to be the first domain where the environment, the data, and the user base all matured together. The interesting question for me is what the next domain is that gets those three things lined up, because once that happens the same kind of fast takeoff should repeat.

r002.rationale: It identifies GitHub as a large part of the pretraining corpus, but does not say that this corpus enables construction of many coding environments.

r003.rationale: It describes engineers as precise and tolerant users who co-develop tools, but does not attribute product growth to coding users having relatively uniform needs.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two reinforcing trends: models are getting better at coding, and products are getting better at turning that capability into useful work.

Coding is particularly well suited to AI because there’s a relatively clear feedback loop. A model can write code, run it, see an error, and try again. Tests don’t tell you whether everything is correct, but they provide much more concrete feedback than you get for many open-ended tasks. That helps both when training a model and when building an agent that can improve its answer through interaction.

At the product level, the shift from autocomplete to agents is significant. If a model only suggests the next few lines, the human still has to carry the whole task forward. Once it can search a repository, edit multiple files, and run tests, you can delegate a larger piece of work. The underlying model matters, but so does the environment you give it: what tools it can use, what context it sees, and how it gets feedback.

There’s also a strong incentive to make this work. Developers use these tools frequently, can recognize when they’re useful, and can build better tools themselves. So capability improvements get translated into products very quickly, and product usage reveals the next set of problems to solve.

I’d still distinguish generating code from doing software engineering. Writing a function with a clear specification is one thing. Understanding an ambiguous request, making the right architectural choice, and maintaining a system over time are harder. I think the rapid progress comes partly from how favorable coding is as an environment, while the next challenge is expanding how much responsibility you can reliably delegate.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention GitHub’s code corpus or constructing coding environments from it.

r003.rationale: The response notes frequent developer use and rapid product iteration, but does not identify uniformity in users’ coding needs as a cause.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two reinforcing trends. One is that models are getting better at coding, and the other is that products are getting better at turning that capability into useful work.

Coding has a particularly good feedback loop. A model can write some code, run it, see an error, and try again. You don’t have to judge every answer purely by whether it looks convincing; you can often test whether it works. That makes coding a natural setting for improving models through interaction with an environment.

But a better model alone doesn’t explain the product progress. There’s a big difference between suggesting the next few lines and helping complete a task. To complete a task, the system needs to find the relevant files, understand the existing implementation, make changes, run tests, and revise its approach. The tools and the way you organize that process matter a lot.

These two sides reinforce each other. As models become more capable, you can give them more autonomy. As products provide better context and feedback, the same model can accomplish more.

I’d still distinguish writing code from doing software engineering. Generating a function is relatively well defined. Understanding what someone actually wants, making a change across a large codebase, and knowing whether the result is ready to ship are harder. So I think the rapid progress is real, but the interesting question is increasingly how much of that whole process the system can reliably take responsibility for.
